title: One-shot Conditional Sampling: MMD meets Nearest Neighbors
one_liner: CGMMD learns to draw samples for a requested condition in one pass by matching generated conditional output laws to real local neighborhoods from the training data.
lead: Conditional sampling asks for outputs tied to an input condition. Given a blurry image, produce a clean version. Given observed measurements, draw plausible hidden parameters. The difficult part is that we rarely observe the full conditional law (the set of possible outputs for each input and how likely each one is). We only see paired examples. CGMMD turns this into a direct matching problem. For a requested condition, it looks at nearby training conditions, treats their outputs as a local stand-in for the true conditional law, and trains a generator so that one forward pass already matches that local law under a kernel score. The result is a one-shot sampler: no optimization loop, no adversary, and no repeated refinement at use time.

problem.h2: We want many plausible outputs for one condition, not one average answer
paras: In conditional generation, one input can correspond to many valid outputs. A noisy image can map to several clean images that differ in fine detail. A set of physical measurements can map to several hidden causes that all fit the data. A model that predicts only one answer often collapses these possibilities into an average and loses the real uncertainty.

Many modern methods attack this with heavy machinery, such as adversarial training or slow iterative sampling. Those methods can work, but they raise test-time cost and training instability. This paper asks whether we can train a direct sampler that emits conditional samples in one pass while still converging to the true conditional law.

callout.html: The method needs to learn a whole conditional law from finite paired data, even though that law is never observed directly.

steps.text: For each training condition, retrieve nearest neighbors among the observed conditions.

steps.b: Use their outputs as local evidence
steps.text: Treat the outputs paired with those neighbors as an measured conditional sample set, which means a finite stand-in for the unknown true law.
Feed the condition and random noise into a generator to produce candidate outputs directly.
Use maximum mean discrepancy, which is a kernel-based distance between sample sets, to compare generated outputs with the neighbor-based reference set.
Adjust the generator so that for many conditions, its output spread matches the observed local spread.

paras: The paper changes the target used for training. Instead of asking the generator to copy one observed output, it asks the generator to match a local set of plausible outputs gathered from nearest conditions.
object.object: the training target for conditional generation

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: local conditional mismatch
hidden.name: How different the generated sample set is from the true output spread for that condition
paras: The main quantity is not pixel error or pointwise error. It is the gap between two sets of samples: the set produced by the generator for a condition and the set that should have come from the true conditional law. Because the true law is unknown, the paper estimates this gap through nearby observed conditions.

This matters because conditional generation is about spread, not just center. A model can predict the average output very well and still fail as a sampler if all of its draws look nearly the same. By comparing sample sets rather than single points, CGMMD trains the generator to reproduce uncertainty and multi-modality, which means several distinct valid modes of output.

heat.caption: The dark cells control whether the generator captures the full output spread for each condition.

reads.html: The hidden number asks whether the generator produces the right range of plausible outputs for this condition, not merely one acceptable guess.
The paper bounds the loss of the CGMMD sampler and proves convergence by combining nearest-neighbor estimates of local conditional laws with MMD matching.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: nearby conditions reveal a local target law
paras: The method works because nearby conditions often have similar conditional behavior. If two noisy images are close in feature space, the spread of clean images that could explain them is also likely to be close. That gives the model a practical way to approximate an unseen conditional law from finite data: look at neighbors and pool their observed outputs.

The MMD loss matters because it compares whole sample sets through a kernel, which means a similarity rule that becomes large when two outputs are close and small when they are far apart. This lets the generator match multi-peaked output sets without choosing one fixed pairing between generated samples and observed outputs. A one-to-one regression target would force the generator toward an average. The set-level comparison avoids that collapse.

The one-pass generator matters because all the heavy work is shifted into training. Once the generator has learned how each condition maps to an output spread, a fresh condition only needs one forward pass with random noise to produce a sample. That is why the paper can target settings such as image denoising and simulation-based posterior estimation, which means drawing hidden causes from observed data, where repeated sampling cost matters.

math.h2: The equation: generated set should match neighbor set
math.words: Training minimizes a distance between two sample sets: generator outputs for one condition and outputs borrowed from nearby observed conditions.
symbols: a distance between two sample sets built from a kernel similarity rule
samples produced by the generator for condition x
observed outputs attached to conditions near x in the training data

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose condition x has three nearest neighbors whose outputs are 2, 3, and 6.
The generator for x currently emits 1, 3, and 7.
The sample sets overlap partly around 3 but differ at the low and high ends.
The MMD score is therefore above zero, so training moves the generator toward the neighbor-based set.
When the generator later emits 2, 3, and 6 more often, the MMD score falls.

math.note: The exact kernel choice affects sensitivity, but the structural idea is unchanged: compare sets of draws, not single paired outputs.

bars.h2: What CGMMD is trying to improve

charts.title: Point prediction or slow iterative sampler
charts.note: Older choices often force a tradeoff between diversity, speed, and simple training.

charts.title: CGMMD
charts.note: The paper's claim is that local neighbor targets plus MMD matching keep the sampler direct without reducing it to average prediction.

items.html: If the feature space does not place similar conditions near each other, the borrowed output sets will describe the wrong local law and the generator will learn the wrong spread.
A weak generator may ignore the noise input and emit nearly the same output each time, which reduces conditional diversity even if the training target is set-based.
If the kernel is too narrow, small differences dominate the score; if it is too broad, distinct modes blur together, so the MMD signal becomes less useful.
Use conditioning features that preserve local similarity, check whether neighbors share similar outputs, and verify that repeated draws for one condition genuinely vary.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic two-mode conditional problem where each input maps to one of two output clusters. Train a one-point regressor, a slow iterative baseline, and CGMMD. For each test input, draw several outputs and compare the output set with the known conditional law. The demo should show that CGMMD reaches both modes in one pass because the neighbor-based target teaches the generator the local spread rather than a single average.
demo.closing: The visible success case is simple: repeated draws for one condition should cover the right modes without running a long sampling chain.
